title: What Happens to Your Body When You Hold Your Breath?
description:
Your lungs hold enough oxygen for about four minutes, so why do most people give up after one? The answer is carbon dioxide, a stubborn muscle, and a reflex you share with diving mammals.

Sources:
- Frontiers in Physiology (2021), Large Lung Volumes Delay the Onset of the Physiological Breaking Point During Simulated Diving: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8511405
- Scientific American, The Limits of Breath Holding: https://scientificamerican.com/article/the-limits-of-breath-holding

This video is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice.

scenes.narration: Take a deep breath and hold it. Right now, your body is already starting a countdown, and the alarm it's waiting for might surprise you.
scenes.headline: HOLD YOUR BREATH

visual.note: person with puffed cheeks holding their breath

scenes.narration: Your lungs hold enough oxygen to keep you going for about four minutes. Yet most people give up after roughly one. So if you're not out of oxygen, what makes you quit?
scenes.headline: FOUR MINUTES OF OXYGEN

visual.note: clean anatomical illustration of the lungs

scenes.narration: Every second, your cells keep making carbon dioxide, and it builds up in your blood. Meanwhile, your breathing rhythm never stops. You're fighting it by holding your diaphragm still, and that strained muscle keeps sending louder and louder signals.
scenes.headline: THE REAL ALARM: CARBON DIOXIDE
scenes.sub: Plus a diaphragm that wants to move

visual.spec: timeline of a breath hold: carbon dioxide level rising, oxygen level falling slowly, diaphragm signals growing, ending at a marked breaking point

scenes.narration: Here's a twist. Dip your face in water while you hold your breath, and your heart slows down. It's called the diving response, a reflex thought to help your body save oxygen.
scenes.headline: YOUR HEART SLOWS DOWN

visual.note: calm swimmer underwater in a clear pool

scenes.narration: Finally, you hit the breaking point. Your automatic rhythm wins, and air rushes back in. On dry land, for healthy adults, that happens long before oxygen runs dangerously low.
scenes.headline: THE BREAKING POINT

visual.note: person taking a big relieved breath

scenes.narration: Follow Inside Your Body for more of the science of you.
